appraisal_events.evidence: When the duchesse comes to dinner, the princesse de Parme closes her door to her own regular guests and has unexpected visitors turned away so as not to displease the 'exigeante duchesse'; conversely, when the princesse dines at the duchesse's she is only afraid of failing to please, understand, or keep up, having already imitated Oriane's dresses and strawberry tarts without matching her success.
appraisal_events.explanation: The duchesse's preferences visibly reorganize the princesse de Parme's household and calendar, while the princesse remains anxiously dependent on winning Oriane's approval and imitates her without equaling her draw — a clear local dominance of the duchesse over the princesse.

appraisal_events.evidence: Swann judged Brichot a pedant and Elstir a boor, despite the former's learning and the latter's genius, because the 'esprit Guermantes' had infiltrated his judgment; he would never have dared present either man to the duchesse.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator exposes Swann's private verdicts on Brichot and Elstir as products of a borrowed, snobbish standard rather than independent judgment, quietly diminishing Swann's own discernment even while affirming the two men's real learning and genius.

status_effects.explanation: Her visits force the princesse de Parme to close her salon to her regular guests and screen admittance, a witnessed display of the duchesse's precedence and drawing power.
The princesse is shown anxiously dependent on the duchesse's approval, imitating her style without success and fearing she will fail to please, understand, or hold her interest.
Swann's contemptuous private judgments of Brichot and Elstir are shown to stem from an absorbed snobbish code rather than genuine discernment, locally diminishing him.

ambiguities: The passage itself calls 'l'esprit des Guermantes' a purely reputational quality ('aussi inexistante que la quadrature du cercle'), which qualifies but does not reverse E1's local elevation of the duchesse.
Brichot and Elstir are the targets of Swann's private disparagement in E2, but the narrator explicitly affirms their real learning and genius, so no negative status effect is recorded for them.
